newsitem.title: INDIA: Bombay workers strike and mourn for slain leader.
newsitem.headline: Bombay workers strike and mourn for slain leader.

text.p: Indian trade union leader Datta Samant was cremated on Friday amid heavy police security as hundreds of thousands of workers massed on Bombay's streets and called a general strike to protest his mafia-style slaying.

Samant, 65, was shot dead in a city suburb on Thursday by four unidentified gunmen, and police said they suspected inter-union rivalry was behind the killing. Businessmen say organised crime has infiltrated unions in the city of 13 million people, India's bustling commercial capital.
Samant's funeral procession and the strike, which slowed traffic in the city, stayed peaceful on a day already marked by heightened security for a visit by Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda.
Deve Gowda offered the help of the federal police to probe Samant's killing if the Maharashtra state government wants it.
Only a few isolated stone throwing incidents in the city's suburbs were reported, police said.
Workers from the various unions that Samant led during the last three decades thronged the five-km (three-mile) route of the funeral procession.
Grieving workers threw garlands onto a cortege decorated with strings of marigolds and chrysanthemums and which carried a large, coloured portrait of Samant.
Some men climbed trees to get a glimpse of their leader's body laid on a raised platform aboard an open truck.
Several hundred thousand people joined the procession, but only a few hundred mourners were allowed inside the walled crematorium at the suburb of Rajawadi.
Samant's eldest son, Prakash, lit the funeral pyre according to Hindu rites inside a soot-covered asbestos shed sheltered by a banyan tree. Chants of Hindu scriptures filled the air.
"This man has sacrificed everything for workers including his life," one sobbing worker told Reuters.
Workers carried flags showing a rising sun over a clenched fist, the symbol of the Kamgar Aghadi (Workers Front), the main union established by Samant, and banners lauding Samant.
Samant's unions represent nearly one million workers at more than 4,000 industrial units in and around Bombay and other parts of Maharashtra state.

In central Bombay and it's eastern suburbs, where textile mills employing members of Samant's trade unions are concentrated, life was virtually paralysed with shops closed, and buses and taxis off the streets.
Engineering, chemical and textile plants shut down for the day, and schools remained closed.
Shops in other areas were open although fewer buses and taxis were in use. Train services were normal.

Police said Samant and his son, Ganesh, were travelling in a jeep when the attackers fired from a motor-rickshaw in the central suburb of Powai. Samant's son was unhurt but his chauffeur was seriously wounded.

A doctor who became a militant trade unionist, Samant took the spotlight in the early 1980s when he led a two-year strike by textile workers in Bombay. He later became a member of the Maharashtra state legislature and the national parliament.
